newsitem.title: FRENCH GUIANA: French Guiana police take over riot-torn Cayenne.
newsitem.headline: French Guiana police take over riot-torn Cayenne.

text.p: French riot police began taking control of the centre of Cayenne in French Guiana early on Wednesday, pushing back demonstrators to the outskirts and dispersing crowds, witnesses said.

Two hundred paramilitary riot police reinforcements were flown in from Paris over the weekend to help quell violence that has flared since last week in France's territory on the northeast coast of South America.

Local police have been overwhelmed by the rioting, which on Thursday and Friday nights left one dead, at least six injured and caused millions of dollars in damage to government buildings and shops in the capital Cayenne.

Violence raged for several hours late on Tuesday with police firing tear gas grenades to disperse crowds. Fresh violence erupted when a magistrate's court convicted seven people arrested during riots last week, witnesses said.

At the announcement of the verdict, bands of youths began to overturn garbage cans, break store windows and attempted to charge the local courthouse. Police fired several rounds of tear gas to disperse the crowd, which had massed near the courthouse all day.
Preliminary reports of damage during Tuesday's violence was estimated to be much lighter than last week's riots, local state-owned radio said.
Airport officials told Reuters all incoming and outgoing flights at French Guiana's international airport near Cayenne would be cancelled on Wednesday.

The airport closure was triggered by a general strike called for Wednesday by an interunion group protesting French government policy in French Guiana and the arrest of the seven rioters convicted on Tuesday.
High school students protesting against poor conditions in local schools sparked the riots when their strike degenerated into clashes between police and youths.
Earlier on Tuesday, the French government said in Paris it would hold wide-ranging talks next year on the situation in French Guiana.

Jean-Jacques de Peretti, minister of overseas territories, said he would visit Guiana shortly with Education Minister Francois Bayrou and organise a conference there next year, "because the future of the Guianese is a matter for the Guianese themselves."
De Peretti told the National Assembly that the problems of French Guiana stemmed largely from illegal immigration and a sharp increase in population to 140,000 from 80,000 over the past 13 years.

French Guiana is the only non-independent territory in South America. Its economy lags behind that of mainland France, and it has an unemployment rate approaching 25 percent of the labour force. Joblessness is particularly acute among the young.
